c.tagline: Benin's quiet official capital of royal palaces, Vodun heritage, and lagoon calm, overshadowed by bustling Cotonou.

taxi.fareNote: Almost all rides are by zemidjan (motorcycle taxi) or shared taxi with no meters; agree on the price in CFA francs before setting off.

emergency.note: 118 reaches the fire brigade; response times can be slow outside the city center, so hotels and clinics are often the fastest first call.

avoid.reason: Petty theft can occur around Ouando and Grand Marché market areas; avoid zémidjan motorbike-taxi rides late at night.

hood_desc: Home to the National Assembly and the Ethnographic Museum's Yoruba masks and royal artifacts; the natural first stop for understanding Beninese and Yoruba history.
The historic royal quarter around King Toffa's Palace (Honmé Museum), on UNESCO's tentative list; suits travelers focused on Beninese royal and Vodun heritage.
A quiet residential district built by returning Afro-Brazilian former slaves, known for Portuguese-style facades and the Da Silva Museum of Beninese-Brazilian history.
The working port and market district on the lagoon, where canoes and zemidjans converge around Porto-Novo's largest market; best for travelers wanting an authentic, unpolished feel.

water.note: Stick to bottled or treated water throughout Benin.

transit.hours: No fixed schedule; zemidjans and shared taxis run informally from early morning to late evening, thinning out after dark.
transit.pay: Cash only (CFA francs), negotiated per ride before departing; there is no fare card or ticketing system.
transit.note: Porto-Novo has no formal public transit network. Zemidjans (motorcycle taxis) are the main way to get around the city, supplemented by shared taxis and bush taxis to Cotonou and other towns; canoes still cross the lagoon to nearby villages.

bus: Shared taxis/bush taxis to Cotonou and regional towns
ferry: Lagoon canoe (pirogue) crossings to nearby lakeside villages

tip.r: Not part of local custom; rounding up small amounts is appreciated at tourist-oriented restaurants and hotels but never expected.

food.name: Akassa
food.desc: Fermented maize dough steamed in leaf parcels into a soft, tangy loaf - the everyday starch, torn by hand and dipped into fish or tomato sauce.

food.desc: Fulani cow's-milk cheese from Benin's north, sliced and pan-fried until golden and squeaky, then eaten with chilli sauce or in a tomato stew.

landmarks: Musee Honme (Royal Palace of King Toffa)
The walled palace compound of King Toffa I reveals the court life of the Gun kingdom before French colonization, room by ceremonial room.
Grande Mosquee de Porto-Novo
A former Afro-Brazilian church turned mosque, its candy-striped baroque facade is one of West Africa's most surprising and photogenic buildings.
Musee Ethnographique Alexandre Senou Adande
Yoruba Gelede masks, ritual objects and royal regalia illuminate the intertwined Yoruba, Gun and vodun cultures of southern Benin.
Musee da Silva
Set in an Afro-Brazilian family mansion, this museum tells the story of formerly enslaved returnees from Brazil who shaped Porto-Novo's architecture and identity.
Place Jean Bayol and King Toffa Statue
The proud statue of King Toffa overlooks this palm-shaded square, the ceremonial gateway between the colonial quarter and the old town.
Palais des Gouverneurs
This handsome domed colonial Governors' Palace, seat of Dahomey's administration and later Benin's parliament, presides over gardens near the lagoon.
Cathedrale Notre-Dame de l'Immaculee Conception
The century-old Catholic cathedral's warm ochre facade rises above the old town, testament to the city's layered mosaic of vodun, Islam and Christianity.
Centre Songhai
A pioneering sustainable-farming campus offers tours of its fish ponds, biogas systems and craft workshops, a hopeful model for African agroecology.
Marche d'Adjarra
Held every four days in a village just outside town, this sprawling market brims with drums, pottery, palm wine and vodun paraphernalia.
Marché International d'Ouando
A large, chaotic market on the edge of Porto-Novo where traders sell everything from produce to textiles and household goods.

train.note: Benin has no regular passenger trains. The OCBN branch line from Cotonou to Porto-Novo was reopened to passengers in 1999 but the service has since ceased, and the main Cotonou-Parakou northern line has run only sporadic passenger trains since about 2006 despite repeated government promises to restore them. There is no functioning cross-border railway to Nigeria, Togo or Niger, so all travel is by road.

intl.to: Lagos (Nigeria) - via the Sèmè-Kraké border, about 40 km east
intl.op: shared taxis and minibuses from the Porto-Novo gare routière — pay at the gare routière

bus.note: Porto-Novo's gare routière handles shared taxis and minibuses east to Lagos via the busy Sèmè-Kraké crossing and north to Abomey, Pobè and Kétou, with vehicles leaving when full rather than to a timetable and fares paid in CFA francs in cash. Minibuses and taxis to Cotonou run constantly, take about 45 minutes and cost around 600 CFA. For a proper air-conditioned coach you generally go to Cotonou first, 30 km west, where ABC Transport (https://www.abctransport.com/) runs Lagos, Lomé and Accra services and Ivorian and Togolese operators head west along the coastal highway. The Nigerian border is chaotic and slow: get your Nigerian visa in advance, expect several checkpoints, and allow three to five hours to Lagos for a distance of barely 100 km.

intl.to: Lagoon villages around Porto-Novo (Benin) - pirogues from the town waterfront
intl.op: informal local boatmen — pay at the landing, around 2,000 CFA return

ferry.note: Porto-Novo sits on a lagoon rather than the open sea, and there is no scheduled ferry service of any kind. Motorised and paddled pirogues run from the waterfront out to the less-visited lake villages, hired informally on the spot for roughly 2,000 CFA return; they have no timetable, no lifejackets and stop at dusk. The better-known stilt village of Ganvié is visited from Abomey-Calavi near Cotonou, not from Porto-Novo. Benin's ocean coast at Cotonou handles cargo only and has no passenger sailings.

half.name: Ganvie
half.blurb: Africa's largest stilt village stands over Lake Nokoue, where Tofinu families paddle dugouts between floating markets, an unforgettable half-day excursion.
